Senses.Note: The first graph also appears as the common variant "sink" (沉): "sink into emptiness and stick in stillness" (沉空滯寂) occurs 30 times in 21 allowlisted texts. The assigned form with "sink" (沈) remains the headword because it is independently attested across nine texts. Both spellings are condemnatory in the sampled Chan contexts; neither names anything the speakers recommend.

Yuwang Duanyu is the exact speaker: in his own instruction he contrasts positing one thing as iron walls and silver mountains with positing the many things as absent and everywhere sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence.

sink in emptiness and remain stuck in stillness
sink into the empty and stagnate in stillness
Senses.Explanation: Speakers use this paired verb phrase for a criticized arrest: sinking into emptiness and remaining stuck in stillness. Stored cases call it an illness, place it among explicit prohibitions, describe self-only concern that neglects living beings, or contrast it with treating the many things as absent. The Chinese Chan sources use it to identify a failure, not to name an activity they commend. Fozhi Duanyu sets two obstructions against each other: "if one teaching exists, layer upon layer of iron walls and silver mountains; if the myriad teachings are absent, everywhere one sinks into emptiness and sticks in stillness" (一法若有重重鐵壁銀山，萬法若無處處沈空滯寂). Gaofeng includes the phrase among a long series of proposed reasons for failure, asking, "is it sinking into emptiness and sticking in stillness?" (莫是沈空滯寂麼), before rejecting the whole diagnostic list as the answer. Yuansou says figures in an arhat painting "sink into emptiness and stick in stillness, know only their own completion, and do not attend to delivering living beings" (沈空滯寂，只知自了，不顧度生). Chushi explicitly calls it "the Chan illness of the two vehicles" (二乘禪病).
